https://www.politico.eu/article/chinas-l.text: VILNIUS — China’s latest trade restrictions on EU companies are unlikely to hurt much — for now. But its choice of targets shows how Beijing could make future retaliation far more painful. China hit 14 EU entities last month with export curbs on so-called dual-use items that have both civilian and military uses. Beijing’s move amounted to a tit-for-tat retaliation after the EU listed the same number of Chinese companies in July in a round of Russia-related sanctions for allegedly aiding Vladimir Putin’s four-year-old war against Ukraine. While five European companies that were listed told POLITICO they would be able to cope with the measures, Beijing’s choice of targets has experts and business leaders worried that any future restrictions would expose Europe’s dependence on China for the supply of critical industry inputs. Advertisement Advertisement “It’s sending a signal. Just think twice: Would you be able to further conduct that business without supplies from China?” Aldas Juronis, CEO of specialized laser company Ekspla, said in an interview. Ekspla is among the 14 EU firms now barred from receiving Chinese dual-use items. The measures come at a critical time. Brussels and Beijing are locked in tense trade negotiations over ways to narrow the EU’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China. In the EU’s view, China’s heavy subsidies for its exporters are driving many European industries out of business and the EU wants to convince China to curb exports to the bloc . Brussels wants to achieve results by the time European leaders meet for their next summit in mid-October. Formally, Beijing said it was retaliating after Brussels listed 14 Chinese-registered companies for aiding the circumvention of EU sanctions on Russia; its list dropped just 24 hours after the EU announcement. Several of the European players cited are active in the defense sector, like Germany’s Rheinmetall and Czechia’s Tatra Trucks. “We firmly reject the link that China has made with the listing by the EU of Chinese entities,” a European Commission spokesperson said, adding that the Chinese entities targeted had been “found to be assisting the Russian military-industrial complex in their illegal invasion of Ukraine.” Advertisement Advertisement The Commission also said it had informed China ahead of time, but Beijing “did not engage with the EU.” Tit for tat “They did this very symmetric,” said Una Aleksandra Bērziņa-Čerenkova, a specialist in Russia-China relations and director of the Latvian Institute of International Affairs. “They didn’t go with an asymmetric list of 100 entities. They’re like: ‘Oh, you like the number 14? Sure, I can play that game.’” Seven of the 14 entities responded to a list of questions from POLITICO; five are privately owned companies, while one is a university and one a public-private lab. All of the companies said they would weather the restrictions without difficulty, with no impact on their bottom lines. A production line is seen inside a clean room at the AT&S production facilities in Leoben, Austria on Aug. 11, 2026. | Kerstin Joensson/AFP via Getty Images The two research institutions — a Polish technical university and a French semiconductor lab — indicated they were still assessing the consequences. Because Ekspla imports only 8 percent of its components from China, CEO Juronis said the company would manage. “If we wouldn’t have been prepared at all, then of course it would be harming us very significantly,” he said, adding that the company had used the lessons it absorbed from the Covid pandemic. Ekspla makes advanced lasers, supplying them mostly to scientists and industrial customers. “We do not have — nor are planning to have — any product which could be used for kinetic applications,” Juronis explained. The Lithuanian company counts medical-device makers and the semiconductor industry among its customers. Advertisement Advertisement The price of autonomy The larger and more prominent companies on Beijing’s list are directly involved in making defense equipment. Rheinmetall, which makes armored vehicles, artillery, ammunition and air defense systems, said in a statement that its “dependence on China had already been significantly reduced in the past.” Similarly, Czech truck manufacturer Tatra and Dutch naval shipyard Koninklijke IHC said they would not be affected by the measures. In April, China had already listed seven EU defense-related companies . In the longer term, however, the list signals to Brussels that building independent European semiconductor and electrification supply chains will come at a price. The semiconductor value chain is well represented in the list, not only by Ekspla. Vigo Photonics from Poland, which makes infrared sensors for chip manufacturing, was also listed by Beijing. And in France, China singled out public-private joint venture III-V Lab , which researches and tests new semiconductors. InPACT Semiconductor, another French company on the list, is a supplier for the lab. Perhaps the most surprising listing is that of the Wrocław University of Science and Technology. The institution conducts research on quantum chips and is involved in Poland’s national quantum laboratory, NLPQT. For Bērziņa-Čerenkova, adding a university is another signal from Beijing. “The EU is increasingly talking about research security and how China is using research cooperation to gain innovation in its defense sector,” she said. Advertisement Advertisement Moreover, China has learned that “weaponizing its economic superiority” can work in its favor, as Bērziņa-Čerenkova put it, pointing to last year’s export curbs on rare earth elements . Some of the companies listed need metals like neodymium, which they predominantly source from China. Turning up the heat Then there’s Lithuania’s Taiwan saga. Vilnius allowed the democratically governed island to open a de facto embassy under the name “Taiwan” in 2021, leading China to downgrade diplomatic relations . Along with Lithuania’s other products, Ekspla’s lasers got stuck quite literally in a Chinese warehouse as a result because Chinese customs no longer recognized Lithuania as a country of origin. While trade has somewhat normalized, Juronis said it was “obvious” that Beijing was going to list at least one Lithuanian company. “It would be strange if they would not include anybody from Lithuania,” he said. “Unfortunately it’s us.” The European Commission spokesperson said the EU executive would raise the issue with the Chinese Ministry of Commerce in the near future and has already requested that all firms be “withdrawn from China’s export control list.” The real lesson from the episode? China’s economic leverage over Europe isn’t a single-shot weapon, as Western governments may have believed before Beijing curbed rare earth exports. “It’s not one bullet, it’s a knob,” Bērziņa-Čerenkova said. “You turn the heat up and you can pressure others into doing what you want. This is a taste of what’s to come.” Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP View image in fullscreen Visitors ride on a rollercoaster at Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, California, in April 2021. Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP Georgia One dead and more injured after incident on Six Flags rollercoaster in US Six Flags Over Georgia ‘deeply saddened’ by tragedy, reportedly occurring on Goliath coaster with 175ft drop Guardian staff and agency Mon 12 Oct 2026 19.51 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 19.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google One person has died and several others were injured in an incident involving a Six Flags rollercoaster on Monday afternoon in Georgia , according to police. The incident took place a Six Flags Over Georgia , about 15 miles (25km) north-west of Atlanta, according to the Cobb county police department. Officials did not confirm how the person died or what caused the others to be injured. However, multiple outlets reported a person had fallen from the park’s Goliath rollercoaster, citing eyewitnesses and anonymous local officials . Six Flags permanently shuts down X2 rollercoaster after claims of brain injuries Read more The rollercoaster, which was introduced at the park in 2006, has a top speed of 70mph (110km/h) and a 175ft drop. A Six Flags spokesperson said the park and local authorities responded immediately and that they are fully cooperating with local authorities as they investigate the incident. “We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today,” the spokesperson said. Late last month, Six Flags Magic Mountain, in southern California, announced that it was retiring its famous X2 rollercoaster amid lawsuits alleging serious brain injury caused by the ride. Six Flags recently settled a wrongful-death lawsuit from the family of a 22-year-old man who died after riding the coaster in 2022, and three more lawsuits alleging traumatic brain injuries were filed last week. Waves crash into coastal homes in Long Beach, California, on Monday. Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP View image in fullscreen Waves crash into coastal homes in Long Beach, California, on Monday. Photograph: Jae C Hong/AP California California coastal homes battered and bruised after weekend of intense waves and flooding Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected Dani Anguiano and Gabrielle Canon Tue 13 Oct 2026 17.29 EDT First published on Tue 13 Oct 2026 14.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes. The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit Mexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction. Footage showed massive waves crashing into Long Beach homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to flee. The damage to homes was significant, leaving some at risk of collapse. Waves from tropical storm Rachel destroy beachfront houses - loop At least nine have been deemed unsafe to enter, the Long Beach Post reported, meaning displaced residents cannot return to retrieve personal items. The storm has cost the city more than $1m from its emergency reserves, according to the outlet. Farther south, the city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency and briefly closed piers to “protect public safety”, citing “higher-than-normal surf” that inundated streets. By Monday, cleanup work was under way and Newport Beach had reopened the piers, but officials advised residents to exercise caution near the water. In Las Vegas, a raging torrent of water rushed over a street near the strip, and the city tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October with 1.08in (2.74cm) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the US National Weather Service. The impacts are just a taste of what’s to come across southern California as a historic El Niño unfolds in the Pacific, threatening to unleash severe storms across the region this winter. View image in fullscreen Waves crash into homes and a sea wall in Long Beach on 12 October 2026. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images Already, the last five hurricanes in the Pacific all reached major status and saw with winds of at least 111mph (178.6 km/h), and one set a record for time spent at category 5. “This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful,” Phil Klotzbach, a Colorado State University researcher who forecasts and studies storm activity, told the Associated Press, adding that the last month has been “berserk”. The El Niño climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the potential to supercharge extreme weather around the world. While it’s expected to strengthen through the end of this year and into next, the excess warmth already measured is climbing off the charts. Forecasters have warned its effects could become exceptionally destructive. In California – especially in the southern part of the state – El Niños typically carry higher risks of severe storms, and with them elevated threats from landslides, debris flows and flash floods. These dangers become more pronounced around recent burn scars, adding hazards to several areas, including in the neighborhoods still recovering from the 2025 Los Angeles firestorm and swaths of Big Sur above Highway 1. View image in fullscreen An emerging El Niño and oceanic Kelvin wave moving up the coastline have compounded conditions in the California region. Photograph: Mario Tama/Getty Images “This year’s tilt in the odds toward wet and stormy conditions in California will be profoundly unsubtle,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said in a recent analysis, adding that its unlike anything he’s observed before. Throughout the winter months, El Niño could also add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8in to 12in caused by the climate crisis over the last century, according to Michael Anderson, a state climatologist. Already, El Niño has elevated sea levels up and down the California coast, from the Mexico border up to the San Francisco Bay Area. Warm waters expanding from an extreme marine heatwave combined with a coastally trapped Kelvin wave – a large underwater band of warm water – have already inundated parts of the North American shoreline. More Kelvin waves are likely and California is already bracing for unusually high king tides to hit during holiday weekends this year, arriving near Thanksgiving and Christmas. While the impacts from heavy rains and high surf are each destructive in their own right, when they align and overlap they can cause even more calamity. View image in fullscreen Waves hit a walkway in front of homes in Long Beach, California, on 10 October 2026 as Tropical Storm Rachel approaches. Photograph: William Liang/AP “Between November 2026 and January 2027, I would anticipate multiple significant coastal flood events that are worse in severity and also much more widespread than what we are currently seeing,” Swain said. “Even a moderate storm could bring water levels higher still, and a strong storm would likely produce widespread damaging, and probably historic, coastal flooding.” Meanwhile, as cities across California begin preparations for intense winter weather , there are still months left before the risks from fire begin to subside. The National Weather Service issued fire weather watches for parts of southern California, including in Los Angeles, as seasonal strong, dry winds align with high temperatures. Forecasters warned that there would be “high risk for extreme fire behavior with any new fire starts Thursday through Friday”. With the threat of fire, heat and sea level rise colliding, as the state readies for more incoming effects from El Niño, Kevin McGowan, the director of LA’s office of emergency management, urged residents to be ready. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard,” he said during a recent briefing, – but all hazards.” The Associated Press contributed reporting Explore more on these topics California Mexico US weather Americas West Coast news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.irishtimes.com/food/2026/10/.text: Food Arán Bakery in Kilkenny takes top Blas na hÉireann award for second time Recognition for bakery’s spelt sourdough makes it first food producer to win supreme champion title twice Bart Pawlukojc and Nicole Server-Pawlukojc, owners of Arán Artisan Bakery & Bistro in Kilkenny and two-time winners of the supreme champion title at the Blas na hÉireann Irish Food Awards. Photograph: Patrick Browne Úna McCaffrey Fri Oct 02 2026 - 19:30 • 2 MIN READ Arán Artisan Bakery & Bistro in Kilkenny has taken the top accolade in the Blas na hÉireann Irish Food Awards for the second time. The bakery, run by couple Nicole Server-Pawlukojc and Bart Pawlukojc, took the supreme champion award for its Arán spelt sourdough, made with 80 per cent local spelt flour from Kells Wholemeal. The bakery, which becomes the first two-time winner, previously took the title in 2022. “To win supreme champion once was an incredible honour, but to come back four years later and win it again is something we never could have imagined,” said Bart Pawlukojc as he accepted the award on Friday evening during the weekend-long Blas na hÉireann event in Dingle, Co Kerry . “There is so much talent and passion in Irish food, so to have our bread recognised at this level is a huge moment for the whole Arán team.” The winning loaf is described as having “a distinctive, slightly nutty flavour, finished with sesame seeds to accentuate the unique characteristics of the grain”. READ MORE Why Halloween pumpkins are smaller this year, and three viral hacks to carve them Affordable wines: a Greek bottle to bid farewell to summer and a French red to greet autumn ‘It’s heartbreaking’: Award-winning Tullamore chocolatier’s stock destroyed by factory fire Restaurant review: Dylan McGrath’s latest offering delivers an expertly executed pizza party [ ‘We moved in with each other after seven days. We got engaged after eight months’ Opens in new window ] From Poland, Pawlukojc and his wife Server-Pawlukojc, from the Philippines, met while working as interns at Noma, the storied restaurant in Copenhagen . They opened Arán in 2019 and have since expanded into a restaurant space across the road, with plans for a nearby tea room now at an advanced stage. Speaking to The Irish Times, Pawlukojc said he was “incredibly proud” of the business and of the Arán team. He and Server-Pawlukojc are lucky to run an “extremely busy” operation, he said, but he described the general business environment as “absolutely horrible” in light of rising costs such as gas bills. “Without debt, we wouldn’t exist,” he said, adding that he worries about other businesses. “If somebody’s not as busy as us, I wouldn’t want to be in their position.” The Blas na hÉireann awards are now in their 19th year. More than 3,000 products were entered across more than 200 food and drink categories. Every county in Ireland was represented. This year’s award for best artisan producer went to Co Cork-based Second Street for its Toffee Popcorn Brittle. Founded by Claire Keane, Second Street Bakeshop specialises in toffee brittle, with an emphasis on simple, natural ingredients. Keane said she was “absolutely thrilled” with the recognition. Artie Clifford, chairperson of Blas na hÉireann, said the standard of entries to the awards had continued to climb this year. “2026 has once again shown us just how exciting and dynamic Ireland’s food and drink industry is,” he said. “Reaching the finalist stage is a remarkable achievement in itself, and to take home a Blas award is brilliant recognition of the hard work and passion that goes into every product.” Join The Irish Times on WhatsApp and stay up to date Get the Food & Drink Club newsletter for the tastiest recipes, reviews and offers Úna McCaffrey Úna McCaffrey is Food & Drinks Editor at The Irish Times Opens in new window Opens in new window Kilkenny Dingle Blas na hÉireann -
